📚 Today you learned

Average Daily Volume (ADV) and Why It Dictates Your Exit Method

ADV is the average number of shares that trade in a name per day. It's the single biggest input into how you should exit a position, and it's exactly why today's SPXC situation is more urgent than a GOOG equivalent would be. GOOG trades tens of millions of shares a day — a market order on 0.3 shares moves nothing, so a plain STOP is low-risk there. SPXC's ADV is a fraction of that — maybe a few hundred thousand shares. On a thinner name, a market order into a fast-moving open can slip meaningfully (see: CAPR's -72% actual fill vs. -36% planned, the exact mechanism that pivoted this whole strategy). The fix on illiquid names isn't "avoid market orders" — it's use an aggressive marketable limit (a limit priced a few percent through the current bid/ask) so you get filled fast without handing a market-maker a blank check.

Also today: Bracket order integrity — an OCA bracket only protects you if you're actually watching for the fill notice; a stop that "should have triggered" and a stop that's confirmed triggered are not the same thing until you've checked.
